intro: Medicine is not only about what doctors can do. It is also about what they should do. In this unit you will meet people whose stories changed the rules: Henrietta Lacks, whose cells were taken without her knowledge; the men of the Tuskegee study, who were denied a known cure; and Dorothea Dix, who used careful evidence to demand better care for people with mental illness.

You will learn the four principles many hospitals use today: autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice. You will see how those principles guide consent, research, organ donation, scarce care and genetic privacy. Then you will turn to the mind: how mental health care has changed, how depression, anxiety and addiction are treated, and how respect for different minds is growing.

By the end, you will be able to explain key cases in medical ethics, weigh arguments on hard questions fairly, describe treatments that have evidence, and know where to find help for yourself or a friend, including 988 and your school counselor.
bigQuestion: How should medicine respect people's rights and minds while trying to help them?

title: Ethics and the Mind

chapters.title: Medical Ethics
chapters.bigQuestion: What do doctors and researchers owe the people they treat and study?

story.title: The Cells That Kept Growing
story.kicker: In 1951 a young mother's cells were taken without her knowledge, and they changed medicine.
paragraphs: Baltimore, 1951. Henrietta Lacks was a 30-year-old mother of five. She grew up farming tobacco in Virginia and later moved to Maryland with her husband. She felt a pain that would not go away, so she went to Johns Hopkins Hospital. It was one of the few hospitals nearby that treated Black patients at the time.

Doctors found cancer on her cervix. During her treatment, a surgeon cut a small sample of the tumor. The sample went to a lab run by George Gey, a scientist who had spent years trying to grow human cells outside the body. Nobody asked Henrietta if her cells could be used this way. Nobody told her family either.

In most labs, human cells died after a few days. Henrietta's cells did something new. They divided again and again and did not stop. The lab named them HeLa, from the first letters of her names. Henrietta died in October 1951. She was 31 years old. Her cells lived on.

HeLa cells were shipped to labs around the world. Scientists used them to test the polio vaccine, study cancer and viruses, and learn how cells work. Companies sold them. For more than 20 years, her family did not know. When they found out, they had hard questions. Who decides what happens to a person's cells? Who should benefit? What should a patient be told?
story.think: Henrietta Lacks's cells helped millions of people. Does that good outcome make it right that no one asked her? Explain your view.

lessons.title: Autonomy and Beneficence
lessons.mainIdea: Good care respects a patient's right to choose and also works for the patient's good.
reading: Picture a 70-year-old man named Mr. Reyes. His doctor recommends heart surgery. Mr. Reyes listens, asks questions, and then says no. He would rather spend his remaining years at home with medicine alone. His doctor disagrees but accepts his choice. This scene shows two ideas that sit at the center of medical ethics.

In 1979 two American scholars, Tom Beauchamp and James Childress, published Principles of Biomedical Ethics. They named four principles that many hospitals now use. The first is *autonomy*. It means a capable adult has the right to make decisions about their own body and care, even choices a doctor would not make. Respecting autonomy means giving honest information and then listening.

The second principle is *beneficence*. It means acting for the patient's good: recommending helpful treatment, relieving pain, and caring for the whole person. Sometimes these two principles pull in different directions. A doctor may believe surgery is best, but the patient decides. In the past, many doctors simply decided for patients. This habit is called *paternalism*, and modern ethics has moved away from it.

words.d: a capable person's right to make decisions about their own body and care
acting for the good of the patient
when a doctor decides for a patient, believing they know best

look.title: Two Principles in One Room
look.text: A doctor tells a 40-year-old woman that a new medicine could lower her blood pressure. The woman says she wants to try diet and exercise first for three months. The doctor thinks the medicine would work faster. She explains the risks of waiting, writes down the plan, and schedules a check-up in three months.
look.prompt: Which of the doctor's actions show beneficence, and which show respect for autonomy?

check.q: Which principle means a capable adult may make decisions about their own care?
check.why: Autonomy is the right of a capable person to decide about their own body and care.

check.q: Who named the four principles in a 1979 book?
check.why: Beauchamp and Childress published Principles of Biomedical Ethics in 1979.

check.q: In the reading, Mr. Reyes refuses surgery and his doctor accepts it. What does this show?
check.why: The doctor disagrees but accepts the patient's own choice, which respects his autonomy.

lessons.title: Do No Harm, Be Fair
lessons.mainIdea: Non-maleficence means avoiding needless harm, and justice means sharing care and burdens fairly.
reading: Every medicine has risks. An antibiotic can cure a bacterial infection, but it can also cause an allergic reaction. Chemotherapy can shrink a cancer, but it can also make a person very tired and sick. Doctors weigh these risks every day. The goal is not zero risk, which is impossible. The goal is that the likely good clearly outweighs the likely harm.

This is the principle of *non-maleficence*, often summed up as "first, do no harm." The phrase is linked with the Hippocratic tradition of ancient Greece, though the exact words do not appear in the oath itself. Non-maleficence tells doctors not to give treatments that are useless or more harmful than helpful, and not to cause pain without a good reason.

The fourth principle is *justice*. It means treating people fairly and sharing both the benefits and the burdens of medicine. Justice asks hard questions. Who gets a scarce organ? Should people with less money wait longer for care? Should one group carry the risks of research while another enjoys the results? You will see these questions again in this chapter.

words.d: the duty to avoid causing needless harm
treating people fairly and sharing the benefits and burdens of medicine fairly
the chance that something harmful may happen

look.title: Weighing Good and Harm
look.text: A patient with a mild cold asks for an antibiotic. The doctor explains that colds are caused by viruses, which antibiotics do not kill. Taking one would not help the cold. It could cause stomach upset or an allergic reaction, and overuse helps bacteria become resistant.
look.prompt: Which of the four principles best explains why the doctor says no? Could any other principle also apply?

check.q: Which phrase sums up non-maleficence?
check.why: Non-maleficence is the duty to avoid needless harm, often summed up as "first, do no harm."

check.q: Why does the reading say the goal is not zero risk?
choices: Because zero risk is impossible, so good must clearly outweigh harm
Because doctors do not care about risk
Because the law allows any risk
Because risk only matters in research
check.why: Every treatment has some risk; ethics asks whether the likely good clearly outweighs the likely harm.

check.q: Which question is mainly about the principle of justice?
choices: Does this medicine have side effects?
Who should get a scarce organ?
Did the patient agree to surgery?
Is this treatment good for this patient?
check.why: Justice is about fair sharing of benefits and burdens, such as who receives a scarce organ.

lessons.title: Informed Consent
lessons.mainIdea: Informed consent means a patient agrees to care after understanding its purpose, risks, benefits and choices.
reading: Before a teenager gets her wisdom teeth removed, the dentist sits down with her and a parent. He explains what the surgery does, what could go wrong, how long healing takes, and what happens if they wait. He answers questions. Then the parent signs a form. That conversation, not just the signature, is the heart of *informed consent*.

Informed consent has several parts. The patient must get clear information about the purpose, the likely benefits, the risks and the other choices, including doing nothing. The patient must be able to understand it, which may require an *interpreter* or plain language. And the choice must be *voluntary*, meaning free of pressure or threats. A patient may also change their mind later.

Minors usually cannot give full legal consent, so a parent or guardian gives permission. Many doctors still ask the young person for their own agreement, called assent. In an emergency, when a person cannot speak and waiting would cause serious harm, doctors may act without consent. Outside these limits, treating someone without consent is a serious ethical and legal wrong.

words.d: agreeing to care or research after understanding its purpose, risks, benefits and choices
freely chosen, without pressure or threats
a trained person who helps a patient and doctor understand each other across languages
a young person's own agreement to care, alongside a parent's permission

look.title: Is This Consent?
look.text: A patient who speaks only Spanish is handed a four-page consent form in English and told, "Sign here so we can start." She signs. No one explains the procedure, and she does not know she can ask questions or say no.
look.prompt: Which parts of informed consent are missing here? What would you change?

check.q: Which is NOT a part of informed consent?
check.why: Consent must be voluntary; pressure breaks it. The other three are required parts.

check.q: What is assent?
choices: A young person's own agreement alongside a parent's permission
check.why: Assent is a minor's own agreement; the parent or guardian gives the legal permission.

check.q: When may doctors act without consent?
choices: In an emergency when the patient cannot speak and waiting would cause serious harm
Whenever the doctor is sure it is best
When the form is too long
When the patient speaks a different language
check.why: The reading names emergencies as the main exception; language barriers call for an interpreter, not skipping consent.

lessons.title: The Nuremberg Code
lessons.mainIdea: After Nazi doctors' crimes, the 1947 Nuremberg Code said voluntary consent is essential in research.
reading: In 1946 and 1947, in the German city of Nuremberg, 23 defendants stood trial before American judges. Most were doctors. During World War II they had carried out experiments on prisoners in Nazi concentration camps. Prisoners were frozen, infected with diseases and harmed in other ways, without any choice. Many died. This trial is known as the Doctors' Trial.

At the end of the trial in 1947, the judges set out ten principles for experiments on human beings. These became known as the *Nuremberg Code*. Its first principle says the voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential. Other principles say research should aim at real good for society, avoid needless suffering, and let a person stop taking part at any time.

The code marked a turning point. It said a person in a study is a *research subject* with rights, not an object. It did not end all harmful research, as the next lessons show. But it gave the world a clear standard. Later rules, such as the World Medical Association's Declaration of Helsinki in 1964, built on its ideas.

words.d: ten principles for human research set out in 1947 after the trial of Nazi doctors
a person who takes part in a scientific study
a 1964 statement of research ethics from the World Medical Association

look.title: The First Principle
look.text: The voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential.
look.cite: The Nuremberg Code, from the judgment in United States v. Karl Brandt et al., 1947
look.prompt: Why do you think the judges put this rule first, before all the others?

check.q: What event led to the Nuremberg Code?
choices: The trial of Nazi doctors after World War II
check.why: The code came from the 1946–47 Doctors' Trial in Nuremberg.

check.q: According to its first principle, what is absolutely essential?
choices: Voluntary consent of the human subject
check.why: The first principle states that voluntary consent is absolutely essential.

check.q: Which later statement built on the Nuremberg Code?
check.why: The World Medical Association's Declaration of Helsinki (1964) built on the code's ideas.

lessons.title: The Tuskegee Study
lessons.mainIdea: For 40 years, a U.S. government study watched Black men with syphilis without telling them or treating them.
reading: In 1932 the U.S. Public Health Service began a study in Macon County, Alabama, near the town of Tuskegee. About 600 Black men took part. Most were poor sharecroppers. About 400 had *syphilis*, a bacterial infection that can damage the heart, brain and other organs over many years. About 200 did not and served as a comparison group.

The men were told they were being treated for "bad blood." In truth, the study only watched what syphilis did to them over time. In the 1940s, *penicillin* became the standard cure for syphilis. The men were not offered it. Researchers even took steps to keep them from getting it elsewhere. Some men died of the disease, and some wives and children were infected.

In 1972 a Public Health Service worker, Peter Buxtun, gave the story to reporter Jean Heller of the Associated Press, and the study ended that year. The men and their families later won a legal settlement. In 1997 President Bill Clinton formally apologized. The study's legacy includes new research rules and lasting *mistrust* of medicine among many Black Americans, a mistrust rooted in real events.

words.d: a bacterial infection that can harm the heart, brain and other organs over time
an antibiotic that became the standard cure for syphilis in the 1940s
a lack of trust, often based on past harm

look.title: Who Was in the Study
look.cite: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, The U.S. Public Health Service Untreated Syphilis Study at Tuskegee
look.prompt: About what share of all the men had syphilis? Why might researchers have wanted a comparison group?

check.q: Who ran the Tuskegee study?
check.why: The U.S. Public Health Service began and ran the study from 1932 to 1972.

check.q: What was the main ethical wrong after the 1940s?
choices: The men were paid too much
Penicillin, a known cure, was withheld from the men
The study was held in a big city
check.why: Once penicillin became the standard cure, the men were not offered it and were kept from it.

check.q: How did the public learn about the study in 1972?
choices: A court ordered it made public
Peter Buxtun gave the story to AP reporter Jean Heller
check.why: Worker Peter Buxtun took the story to Jean Heller of the Associated Press; Clinton apologized later, in 1997.

lessons.title: Henrietta Lacks and HeLa
lessons.mainIdea: HeLa cells helped medicine enormously, but they were taken without consent, raising questions about fairness.
reading: You met Henrietta Lacks in this chapter's story. Her cells, called HeLa, became the first human cells to keep growing in a lab for a long time. Scientists called them an immortal *cell line*. That means a group of cells that can divide again and again, so many labs can use copies of the same cells.

HeLa cells were used to test the polio vaccine in the 1950s. Later they helped research on cancer, viruses, genes and many medicines. Yet Henrietta was never asked. In 1951, it was common for doctors to use tissue left over from treatment without asking. Her family learned about the cells only in the 1970s. They received no money, while companies sold the cells.

Rebecca Skloot's 2010 book, The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks, made the story widely known. In 2013 the U.S. National Institutes of Health reached an agreement with the Lacks family. Scientists who want to use HeLa *genome* data must now apply, and family members help review the requests. The story raises lasting questions about consent, privacy and who benefits from a person's body.

words.d: a group of cells that can keep dividing in a lab so copies can be shared
the full set of genetic instructions in a living thing
the cell line grown from Henrietta Lacks's tumor in 1951

look.title: Then and Now
look.text: In 1951, doctors often used tissue from patients without asking, and it was not against the rules. Today, most research on human tissue needs a review board's approval and, in many cases, the person's consent. HeLa genome data now has a family voice in who may use it.
look.prompt: Something can be legal and common but still unfair. Using the HeLa story, explain how that can happen.

check.q: What made HeLa cells special?
choices: They kept dividing in the lab for a long time
They came from a famous scientist
They were the first cells ever seen
check.why: HeLa was the first human cell line to keep growing in a lab, so many labs could share it.

check.q: Which vaccine was tested using HeLa cells in the 1950s?
check.why: The reading says HeLa cells were used to test the polio vaccine.

check.q: What did the 2013 NIH agreement do?
choices: Gave the family a role in reviewing requests to use HeLa genome data
Banned all use of HeLa cells
Paid every scientist who used the cells
Made HeLa data free with no review
check.why: Researchers must apply, and family members help review requests for HeLa genome data.

lessons.title: The Belmont Report
lessons.mainIdea: The 1979 Belmont Report set three principles for U.S. research: respect for persons, beneficence and justice.
reading: After the Tuskegee study became public, Congress passed the National Research Act in 1974. The law created a national commission to set clear rules for research with people. The commission met at the Belmont conference center in Maryland. Its short report, published in 1979, is called the *Belmont Report*.

The report names three principles. *Respect for persons* means treating people as able to make their own choices and protecting those who cannot, such as young children. Beneficence means maximizing possible benefits and reducing harm. Justice means sharing the burdens and benefits of research fairly, so that poor or powerless groups are not chosen just because they are easy to use.

The report turned each principle into practice: informed consent, a careful look at risks and benefits, and fair selection of subjects. Today, most U.S. research with people, including all government-funded studies, must be approved by an *institutional review board*, or IRB. An IRB is a committee that checks a study's plan before it starts. When your school or a hospital runs a survey study, an IRB may review it.

words.d: a 1979 U.S. report setting three principles for research with people
treating people as able to choose for themselves and protecting those who cannot
a committee that reviews and approves research with people before it starts

look.title: Be the Review Board
look.text: A researcher wants to test a new pain medicine. She plans to recruit only people in a county jail because they are easy to find and will be paid a small amount. The form explains the risks. People who say no will not be punished.
look.prompt: As an IRB member, which Belmont principle worries you most about this plan, and what would you ask her to change?

check.q: What led Congress to pass the National Research Act in 1974?
choices: The public learning about the Tuskegee study
check.why: The act followed the 1972 exposure of the Tuskegee study and created the commission that wrote the Belmont Report.

check.q: Which is one of the Belmont Report's three principles?
check.why: The three are respect for persons, beneficence and justice.

check.q: What does an IRB do?
choices: Reviews research plans with people before they start
check.why: An institutional review board checks a study's plan before it begins.

lessons.title: Organ Donation
lessons.mainIdea: Transplants save lives, and ethics guides how organs are given and shared.
reading: In 1954 in Boston, surgeon Joseph Murray moved a kidney from one man into his identical twin brother. The brother lived for years afterward. It was the first long-term successful kidney *transplant*. Murray later shared the Nobel Prize. Today surgeons transplant kidneys, livers, hearts, lungs and other organs.

Most organs come from a *donor* who has died. Some come from living donors, who can give one kidney or part of a liver. In the United States, people can join a donor registry, often when they get a driver's license. Buying and selling organs is illegal under the National Organ Transplant Act of 1984, because payment could pressure poor people and make access unfair.

There are not enough organs for everyone who needs one. The U.S. government reports that more than 100,000 people are on the national waiting list. A national network matches organs using medical need, blood and tissue type, time waiting and distance. Ethics asks that these rules be fair and not depend on wealth or fame. Donation is a personal choice; families can talk it over with each other and a doctor.

words.d: moving an organ or tissue from one person to another
a person who gives an organ, tissue or blood
an official list of people who have agreed to something, such as organ donation

look.title: Why Not Pay Donors?
look.text: Some economists argue that paying kidney donors could shorten waiting lists and save lives. Many ethicists answer that payment would pressure poor people to sell their organs and turn the body into a product. U.S. law, and most countries' laws, forbid organ sales.
look.prompt: Give the strongest point on each side. Which principles of ethics does each side lean on?

check.q: What happened in Boston in 1954?
choices: The first long-term successful kidney transplant, between twins
The start of the donor registry
check.why: Joseph Murray transplanted a kidney between identical twins in 1954.

check.q: Why does U.S. law ban buying and selling organs?
choices: Payment could pressure poor people and make access unfair
check.why: The 1984 law aims to prevent pressure on poor people and unfair access.

check.q: Which factor does the matching system use?
choices: How much money the patient has
check.why: Matching uses medical need, blood and tissue type, waiting time and distance, not wealth or fame.

lessons.title: Sharing Scarce Care
lessons.mainIdea: When there is not enough care for all, ethics asks for clear, fair rules decided ahead of time.
reading: A bus crash sends 20 injured people to a small hospital at once. There are only a few surgeons. Staff quickly sort patients: who needs help right now, who can wait, and who has minor injuries. This sorting is called *triage*, from a French word meaning to sort. It began on battlefields and is now used in every emergency room.

Sometimes the shortage lasts longer. In the spring of 2020, some hospitals worried they would run out of breathing machines called *ventilators* for COVID-19 patients. Many states and hospitals wrote crisis plans. These plans tried to save the most lives while treating people equally, but they also stirred debate. Critics worried that some rules could treat older or disabled people unfairly.

Ethicists often say the rules for *allocation*, meaning how scarce resources are shared, should be made in advance, in public and with input from the communities affected. They should use medical facts, not a person's wealth, race or social worth. People still disagree about details, such as whether to consider age or who is a health worker. These remain open, contested questions.

words.d: sorting patients by how urgently they need care
a machine that helps a person breathe
deciding how scarce resources are shared

look.title: Writing the Rules
look.text: Imagine your town has one new medicine and enough doses for only half of the people who could use it. Option A: first come, first served. Option B: a lottery. Option C: those most likely to benefit go first. Option D: health workers go first so they can keep caring for others.
look.prompt: Choose one option or a mix, and explain which ethical principle guides your choice. What might a critic say?

check.q: What is triage?
choices: Sorting patients by how urgently they need care
check.why: Triage comes from a French word meaning to sort and ranks patients by urgency.

check.q: Why did some critics object to certain 2020 crisis plans?
choices: They could treat older or disabled people unfairly
They were written in secret by patients
check.why: The reading notes worry that some rules could be unfair to older or disabled people.

check.q: According to many ethicists, how should allocation rules be made?
choices: By each doctor in the moment
In advance, in public, with community input
check.why: Ethicists often say rules should be made ahead of time, openly, with input from affected communities.

lessons.title: Genetic Testing and Privacy
lessons.mainIdea: Genetic tests can guide care, but genetic information needs careful privacy protection.
reading: A woman's mother and aunt both had breast cancer. Her doctor suggests a *genetic test* for changes in genes called BRCA1 and BRCA2. Certain changes in these genes raise the risk of breast and ovarian cancer. A result can help her and her doctor plan screening. It may also matter to her sisters and children, who share some of her genes.

Genetic information is unusual because it is shared by families and cannot be changed. Many people send saliva to home DNA companies to learn about their ancestry. They may not think about who else could see the data. In some famous cases, police have used public DNA databases to find crime suspects through distant relatives. People disagree about whether that use is fair.

U.S. laws offer some protection. HIPAA, a 1996 law, protects health records held by doctors and insurers. The *Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act*, or GINA, passed in 2008, bans health insurers and most employers from treating people unfairly based on their genes. GINA does not cover life insurance or long-term care insurance. A *genetic counselor* can help people decide whether to test and what a result means.

words.d: a test that looks for changes in a person's genes
a 2008 U.S. law (GINA) that bans health insurers and most employers from genetic discrimination
a trained professional who helps people understand genetic tests and results

look.title: Whose Information Is It?
look.text: A young man takes a home DNA test for fun. The result shows a gene change linked to a higher risk of a heart condition. He wonders whether to tell his brother, who did not take the test and may not want to know.
look.prompt: Should he tell his brother? Use the ideas of autonomy and beneficence in your answer.

check.q: Why is genetic information unusual?
choices: It is shared by families and cannot be changed
check.why: Relatives share genes, and a person's genes do not change.

check.q: What does GINA, passed in 2008, do?
choices: Bans health insurers and most employers from genetic discrimination
check.why: GINA covers health insurance and most employment, but not life insurance.

check.q: Which kind of insurance does GINA NOT cover?
check.why: The reading says GINA does not cover life or long-term care insurance.

review.q: Which of the four principles means acting for the patient's good?
review.why: Beneficence is acting for the patient's good.

review.q: What did the Nuremberg Code and the Belmont Report both stress?
choices: Voluntary, informed consent of research subjects
review.why: Both documents place consent at the center of ethical research.

review.q: Put these in order: Nuremberg Code, Belmont Report, end of the Tuskegee study.
review.why: The code came in 1947, the study ended in 1972, and the report came in 1979.

review.q: What do the Tuskegee study and the HeLa story have in common?
choices: Black Americans were not given full information or a real choice
Both ended with a cure for cancer
Both were approved by an IRB
review.why: In both, Black patients were not told the truth or asked for real consent.

review.q: A hospital sorts crash victims by urgency. What is this called?
review.why: Triage means sorting patients by how urgently they need care.

review.q: Which statement about organ donation in the U.S. is correct?
choices: Organs may be bought and sold
Only living donors can give organs
More than 100,000 people are on the waiting list
review.why: The U.S. government reports more than 100,000 people waiting; organ sales are illegal.

review.q: Which principle is most at stake if a study uses only poor people because they are easy to recruit?
review.why: Justice asks that research burdens not fall on groups chosen because they are easy to use.

review.q: Who can help a person decide whether to take a genetic test?
review.why: Genetic counselors help people understand genetic tests and their results.

chapters.title: Mental Health and the Brain
chapters.bigQuestion: How has our care for the mind changed, and what helps people stay well today?

story.title: Two Visits, 180 Years Apart
story.kicker: A student reads a report from the 1840s and then walks into a school clinic.
paragraphs: Maya's history teacher hands out a copy of a document from 1843. It was written by a Massachusetts teacher named Dorothea Dix and presented to the state legislature. Dix had visited jails and poorhouses across the state. She described people with mental illness kept in cages, cellars and stalls, some in chains, some without clothing, in the cold.

Maya reads slowly. Dix did not only complain. She counted, named towns and wrote down what she saw, visit after visit. Her careful evidence persuaded lawmakers to expand a state hospital. She went on to push other states to build hospitals where people could receive care instead of punishment.

After school, Maya walks past her school's wellness room. It has soft light, a couch and a poster with the number 988. Down the hall, the school counselor's door is open. A classmate is inside, talking. Nobody is in chains. Nobody is hidden away. Help is a hallway away.

Maya writes in her notebook: what changed between 1843 and today? New science about the brain. New treatments. New laws. But also new ideas about respect. She realizes the biggest change may be how people talk about minds that work differently or that are going through a hard time.
story.think: Dix used careful evidence to change laws. What kind of evidence could a student gather today to improve mental health support at school?

lessons.title: Dorothea Dix and the Asylums
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1800s, reformers like Dorothea Dix pushed for hospitals that treated mental illness with care, not punishment.
reading: In 1841 Dorothea Dix volunteered to teach a Sunday class at a jail in East Cambridge, Massachusetts. She found people with mental illness held with criminals in an unheated room. She spent the next two years visiting jails and poorhouses. In 1843 she presented her findings, called a *memorial*, to the Massachusetts legislature.

Dix belonged to a reform movement inspired partly by *moral treatment*. This approach, developed by reformers such as Philippe Pinel in France and the Tuke family in England, held that people with mental illness should be treated with kindness, routine, fresh air and useful work. Dix spent decades asking states to build public hospitals based on these ideas.

Many such hospitals, then called *asylums*, opened in the United States in the 1800s. At first, some offered real care. Over time, many became crowded and underfunded. Patients sometimes stayed for decades with little treatment. The story shows a pattern in history: a good reform can fall short when money, staff and attention run out.

words.d: a formal written statement of facts sent to a government to ask for action
a 1700s–1800s approach that treated mental illness with kindness, routine and useful work
an older name for a hospital for people with mental illness

look.title: Dix Speaks to Lawmakers
look.text: I come to call your attention to people with mental illness in this state who are kept in cages, closets, cellars, stalls and pens, chained, unclothed and beaten into obedience.
look.cite: Dorothea Dix, Memorial to the Legislature of Massachusetts, 1843 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Why might Dix list so many specific places? How does this kind of detail persuade lawmakers?

check.q: What did Dorothea Dix find at the East Cambridge jail in 1841?
choices: People with mental illness held with criminals in an unheated room
check.why: Her visit to the jail began her work; she found people with mental illness kept in poor conditions.

check.q: What was moral treatment?
choices: Treating mental illness with kindness, routine and useful work
check.why: Moral treatment, linked with Pinel and the Tukes, stressed kindness, routine and work.

check.q: What happened to many asylums over time?
check.why: The reading says many became crowded, underfunded and offered little treatment.

lessons.title: Leaving the Big Hospitals
lessons.mainIdea: In the late 1900s, care moved from large hospitals to communities, with gains and real gaps.
reading: By the 1950s, hundreds of thousands of Americans lived in state mental hospitals. Then several changes arrived. In the 1950s, the first effective *psychiatric* medicines, such as chlorpromazine, helped many people with severe symptoms. Journalists and courts exposed poor conditions. Many people argued that patients should live in their own communities.

In 1963 President John F. Kennedy signed the Community Mental Health Act. It aimed to build local mental health centers so people could get care near home. Over the next decades, most large hospitals shrank or closed. This shift is called *deinstitutionalization*. Many people gained freedom, jobs and family life they could not have had in a hospital.

But far fewer community centers were built than planned, and funding often fell short. Some people who left hospitals did not get steady care. Many experts link these gaps to people with mental illness who are unhoused or in jails today. Historians and policy experts still debate how much each cause matters. Building strong *community care* remains unfinished work.

words.d: having to do with the medical care of mental illness
moving people out of large mental hospitals into community living and care
mental health services offered close to where people live

look.title: A Promise Half Kept
look.text: Plan: close big hospitals and open many local clinics. Result: most big hospitals closed. Far fewer local clinics opened than planned. Some people thrived at home. Others had nowhere steady to go for care.
look.prompt: Was deinstitutionalization a success, a failure, or both? Support your answer with one fact from each side.

check.q: What did the 1963 Community Mental Health Act aim to do?
choices: Build local mental health centers so people could get care near home
check.why: The act, signed by Kennedy, aimed at local centers for care near home.

check.q: What is deinstitutionalization?
choices: Moving people out of large mental hospitals into community care
check.why: It names the shift from large hospitals to community living and care.

check.q: What was a main gap in deinstitutionalization?
choices: Far fewer community centers were built than planned
check.why: The reading says fewer community centers were built than planned and funding fell short.

lessons.title: Depression and Anxiety
lessons.mainIdea: Depression and anxiety are common, real health conditions, and they are treatable.
reading: Jordan used to love basketball. For the past month he has felt heavy and tired, sleeps badly and has stopped caring about games. Nothing big happened. His friend Ana feels something different. Before tests, her heart races, her stomach knots and worries loop in her head, even when she has studied well. Both may be describing signs of real health conditions.

*Depression* is more than a sad day. It is a low mood or loss of interest that lasts at least two weeks and affects sleep, energy, appetite, focus or feelings of worth. An *anxiety disorder* involves fear or worry that is strong, lasts a long time and gets in the way of daily life. Both involve the brain and body, and both are shaped by genes, life events and stress.

These conditions are common. The National Institute of Mental Health estimates that in 2021 about one in five U.S. adults lived with some mental illness. Most important, they are treatable. Many people feel much better with therapy, medication, or both, along with steady routines. If you notice signs like these in yourself or a friend, a trusted adult, school counselor or doctor can help.

words.d: a health condition with low mood or loss of interest lasting at least two weeks
a health condition with strong, lasting fear or worry that gets in the way of daily life
a sign that a person notices, such as poor sleep or a racing heart

look.title: How Common? U.S. Adults, 2021
rows: At least one major depressive episode in the year
look.cite: National Institute of Mental Health, Mental Illness statistics (2021 National Survey on Drug Use and Health)
look.prompt: About how many adults out of 100 lived with any mental illness? What does this suggest about how many people you know may need support?

check.q: How long does low mood usually last to be called depression?
check.why: Depression involves low mood or loss of interest lasting at least two weeks.

check.q: Ana's heart races and worries loop before tests even when she has studied. Which condition fits best?
choices: An anxiety disorder, if it is strong, lasting and gets in the way
check.why: Strong, lasting fear or worry that disrupts life describes an anxiety disorder.

check.q: About what share of U.S. adults lived with any mental illness in 2021, according to NIMH?
check.why: NIMH estimates about 23 percent, roughly one in five.

lessons.title: Talk Therapy and CBT
lessons.mainIdea: Cognitive behavioral therapy helps people notice and change thought patterns, and strong evidence supports it.
reading: Ana tells herself, "If I don't get an A, I'm a failure." Her therapist asks her to write down that thought and look for evidence. Has she ever gotten a B and still done well? Yes. Together they write a more balanced thought: "A B would be disappointing, but I can learn from it." Ana practices this each week.

This method is *cognitive behavioral therapy*, or CBT. It was developed in the 1960s by psychiatrist Aaron Beck at the University of Pennsylvania, building on earlier work. CBT teaches that thoughts, feelings and actions affect one another. By learning to spot unhelpful thoughts and try new actions, people can change how they feel. Therapists often give short practice tasks between sessions.

Many controlled studies show that CBT helps with depression and anxiety disorders. It is often a first choice for young people. It is one kind of *psychotherapy*, or talk therapy. Other kinds focus on relationships, family, or skills for handling strong emotions. A good fit between the person and the *therapist* matters a great deal.

words.d: a talk therapy that helps people notice and change unhelpful thoughts and actions
treatment through talking with a trained professional
a trained professional who provides talk therapy

look.title: Catch the Thought
look.text: Situation: a friend does not answer your text for three hours. Thought: "They must be mad at me." Feeling: worried. Action: you stop texting everyone.
look.prompt: Write a more balanced thought for this situation. How might the feeling and action change?

check.q: Who developed cognitive behavioral therapy in the 1960s?
check.why: Psychiatrist Aaron Beck developed CBT at the University of Pennsylvania.

check.q: What is the core idea of CBT?
choices: Thoughts, feelings and actions affect one another
check.why: CBT teaches that changing thoughts and actions can change feelings.

check.q: What does evidence show about CBT?
choices: It only works for broken bones
Many controlled studies show it helps depression and anxiety
It is banned for young people
check.why: The reading says controlled studies support CBT for depression and anxiety disorders.

lessons.title: Medicine and Daily Habits
lessons.mainIdea: Medication can help some conditions, and sleep, movement and connection support every mind.
reading: Jordan's doctor listens carefully and screens him for depression. She suggests therapy first. After some weeks, they talk about adding medication too. She explains that an *antidepressant* may take several weeks to help, can have side effects, and should never be stopped suddenly without talking to her. Jordan and his parents decide together.

One common group of antidepressants is called *SSRIs*. The first widely used one in the United States, fluoxetine, was approved in 1987. Studies show these medicines help many people with moderate or severe depression and some anxiety disorders. For young people, doctors watch closely, especially in the first weeks. Only a prescriber decides on a medicine and its amount.

Daily habits also matter. Regular *sleep*, physical activity, time outdoors and time with people who care about you support mood and focus. Studies show exercise can ease mild to moderate depression. Habits are not a replacement for treatment when someone needs it. They work best as a steady base alongside therapy or medicine. Tell your doctor about any herbs or supplements, since some can interact with medicines.

words.d: a medicine prescribed to help treat depression and some other conditions
a common group of antidepressant medicines
the body's nightly rest, which supports mood, memory and focus

look.title: Building a Steady Base
look.text: A student's week: bed at 1 a.m. most nights, phone until then, no time outside, lunch alone. Another week: bed by 11, a walk after school, lunch with a friend, and one talk with a counselor.
look.prompt: Which habits in the second week support mental health? Which one would be easiest for you to try first?

check.q: What did Jordan's doctor say about antidepressants?
choices: They may take several weeks, can have side effects, and should not be stopped suddenly
They are safe to share with friends
check.why: The doctor explained the time to work, side effects and not stopping suddenly.

check.q: Who decides whether to use a medicine and how much?
choices: A prescriber, such as a doctor
check.why: Only a prescriber decides on a medicine and its amount.

check.q: How do daily habits fit with treatment?
choices: They replace treatment in all cases
They are a steady base that works alongside therapy or medicine
check.why: The reading says habits support mood and work best alongside treatment when needed.

lessons.title: Addiction and the Brain
lessons.mainIdea: Addiction is a treatable brain condition, not a failure of character.
reading: Picture a man who first took pain pills after back surgery. Over months, he needed more to feel the same effect. When he tried to stop, he felt sick and anxious. He kept using even as it hurt his job and family. His story is common. It shows how a substance can change the brain over time.

*Addiction* is a condition in which a person keeps using a substance or doing an activity despite harm. The National Institute on Drug Abuse describes it as a treatable brain disorder. Many drugs flood the brain's reward system with a chemical messenger called *dopamine*. Over time the brain adapts, and cravings grow. Teen brains are still developing, which is one reason early use carries more risk.

Seeing addiction as a health condition changes how we help. Effective treatment includes counseling and, for opioid addiction, medicines such as buprenorphine and methadone, which have strong evidence. *Recovery* is possible, and many people reach it, sometimes after more than one try. Using respectful words, like "a person with a substance use disorder," makes it easier for people to seek help.

words.d: continuing to use a substance or do an activity despite harm, linked to brain changes
a chemical messenger in the brain's reward system
the process of getting well and building a healthy life after addiction

look.title: Two Ways to Speak
look.text: Headline A: "Addict Arrested Again." Headline B: "Man With Substance Use Disorder Needs Treatment, Family Says." Both headlines describe the same person on the same day.
look.prompt: How might each headline shape what readers think should happen next? Which respects the person more, and why?

check.q: How does the National Institute on Drug Abuse describe addiction?
check.why: NIDA describes addiction as a treatable brain disorder.

check.q: What role does dopamine play in addiction?
choices: It is a medicine for opioid addiction
It is a chemical messenger that drugs flood in the reward system
check.why: Many drugs flood the brain's reward system with dopamine, and the brain adapts.

check.q: Which treatments for opioid addiction have strong evidence?
choices: Medicines such as buprenorphine and methadone, with counseling
check.why: The reading names these medicines, along with counseling, as effective.

lessons.title: How Stigma Is Changing
lessons.mainIdea: Stigma keeps people from seeking help, and open talk from public figures is helping change it.
reading: At the Tokyo Olympics in 2021, gymnast Simone Biles withdrew from several events. She explained that she needed to protect her mental and physical health. Some people criticized her. Many more praised her for being honest. Around the same time, other well-known athletes spoke openly about anxiety and depression.

*Stigma* is a set of negative beliefs and labels attached to a group. For mental health, stigma can sound like "just snap out of it" or jokes about people being "crazy." It can lead people to hide what they are going through. Many people with mental health conditions wait years before seeking help, and stigma is one of the reasons.

Stigma is changing through contact and honest stories. When people hear a friend, teacher or athlete describe a hard time and their recovery, fear drops. Schools add mental health lessons. Words matter too. *Person-first language*, such as "a person with depression," puts the person before the condition. Some people prefer identity-first words; asking is a respectful habit.

words.d: negative beliefs and labels attached to a group that can make people feel ashamed
words that name the person before the condition, like "a person with depression"
choosing to share personal information, such as a health condition, with others

look.title: Rewrite the Line
look.text: Overheard in a hallway: "He's so psycho, he freaked out over a test." "She's just being dramatic, everyone gets sad."
look.prompt: Rewrite each line in a way that is accurate and kind. How might the new words change what the listener does next?

check.q: What is stigma?
choices: Negative beliefs and labels attached to a group
check.why: Stigma is a set of negative beliefs and labels that can shame people.

check.q: How can stigma harm people?
choices: It can lead people to hide their struggles and delay help
check.why: The reading says stigma leads people to hide what they face and wait before seeking help.

check.q: Which is an example of person-first language?
check.why: Person-first language names the person before the condition.

lessons.title: Neurodiversity
lessons.mainIdea: Neurodiversity describes the natural variety of human minds, including autistic people and people with ADHD or dyslexia.
reading: In one classroom, Leo notices patterns in numbers that others miss and prefers a quiet corner. Priya thinks fast, has great ideas and does best when she can move. Sam reads more slowly but tells vivid stories out loud. Each of these students' brains works a little differently. Each has real strengths and specific needs.

The word *neurodiversity* is usually credited to Australian sociologist Judy Singer in the late 1990s. It describes the natural variety in how human brains think, learn and sense the world. People whose brains work in less typical ways, such as autistic people or people with ADHD or dyslexia, are often called *neurodivergent*. The idea encourages respect rather than trying to make everyone the same.

The neurodiversity view does not deny that people may need support. Instead it focuses on *accommodations*, changes that help a person learn or work, such as extra time, quiet spaces, audiobooks or movement breaks. In U.S. public schools, laws such as the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act support plans that fit each student. Many neurodivergent people also value community with others who think like them.

words.d: the natural variety in how human brains think, learn and sense the world
having a brain that works in less typical ways, such as autism, ADHD or dyslexia
a change that helps a person learn or work, such as extra time or a quiet space

look.title: Same Goal, Different Paths
look.text: The assignment: show you understand a chapter. Leo writes a detailed chart. Priya records a two-minute video while walking. Sam listens to the audiobook and explains the chapter out loud to the teacher.
look.prompt: Did all three meet the goal? What accommodations helped each one show what they know?

check.q: Who is usually credited with the word neurodiversity?
check.why: The term is usually credited to Australian sociologist Judy Singer in the late 1990s.

check.q: What does neurodivergent mean?
choices: Having an infection of the brain
Having a brain that works in less typical ways
check.why: Neurodivergent describes brains that work in less typical ways, such as autism, ADHD or dyslexia.

check.q: Which is an accommodation?
check.why: An accommodation is a change that helps, such as extra time or a quiet space.

lessons.title: Mindfulness From Buddhist Roots
lessons.mainIdea: Mindfulness began in Buddhist practice and has been studied as a support for stress, anxiety and depression.
reading: A student sits at her desk before a test. She closes her eyes and notices her breath going in and out. When her mind jumps to worries, she gently brings it back to her breath. After two minutes, her shoulders are lower. She is practicing *mindfulness*: paying attention to the present moment on purpose, without judging it.

Mindfulness has deep roots in Buddhism, which began in ancient India about 2,500 years ago. The Pali word sati, often translated as mindfulness, is part of Buddhist teaching on the path to ending suffering. In Buddhism, *meditation* is a spiritual practice within a larger way of life and ethics.

In 1979, Jon Kabat-Zinn began a program at the University of Massachusetts Medical School called *Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction*. It taught mindfulness in a nonreligious way to patients. A 2014 review in JAMA Internal Medicine found moderate evidence that meditation programs can ease anxiety and depression. They are a helpful tool for many people, not a replacement for treatment when someone needs it.

words.d: paying attention to the present moment on purpose, without judging it
a practice of training attention, often by focusing on the breath
an eight-week program started by Jon Kabat-Zinn in 1979 that teaches mindfulness

look.title: What the Review Found
look.text: Mindfulness meditation programs showed moderate evidence of improving anxiety, depression and pain, and low evidence of improving stress and overall quality of life.
look.cite: Goyal and colleagues, Meditation Programs for Psychological Stress and Well-being, JAMA Internal Medicine, 2014 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: What does "moderate evidence" suggest about how sure scientists are? Why is it important to state the strength of evidence?

check.q: Where does mindfulness have deep roots?
check.why: Mindfulness comes from Buddhist teaching; the Pali word is sati.

check.q: What did Jon Kabat-Zinn start in 1979?
check.why: He began MBSR at the University of Massachusetts Medical School.

check.q: What did the 2014 review find?
choices: Moderate evidence that meditation programs can ease anxiety and depression
check.why: The review found moderate evidence for anxiety, depression and pain.

lessons.title: Mental Health Across Cultures
lessons.mainIdea: Cultures describe distress in different ways, and good care listens to a person's own words and beliefs.
reading: A grandmother tells her doctor that her heart feels heavy and her body aches. She does not use the word depression. In her culture, emotional pain is often described through the body. The doctor listens, asks about sleep, mood and family, and learns she has been grieving since her husband died.

Across the world, people explain and express distress differently. In some cultures, people are more likely to describe body symptoms, such as headaches or tiredness. Many Latin American communities name an *ataque de nervios*, a sudden episode of intense emotion, often after family stress. Traditional Chinese Medicine links emotions with the body's organs and the flow of qi, which is the tradition's own idea.

The American Psychiatric Association's manual, the DSM-5, published in 2013, includes a *Cultural Formulation Interview*. It gives clinicians questions to ask about how a person understands their problem and what help they want. Families, faith leaders and traditional healers may matter a lot. *Culturally responsive care* respects these beliefs while offering treatments that have evidence.

words.d: a term used in many Latin American communities for a sudden episode of intense emotion
a set of questions in the DSM-5 to learn how a person understands their problem
health care that respects a person's culture, language and beliefs

look.title: Asking the Right Questions
look.text: Question A: "Do you have depression?" Question B: "What do you call this problem? What do you think caused it? Who in your life helps when things are hard? What kind of help are you hoping for?"
look.prompt: Which set of questions might help the grandmother most, and why?

check.q: How did the grandmother describe her feelings?
choices: Through her body, like a heavy heart and aches
check.why: In her culture, emotional pain is often described through the body.

check.q: What is the Cultural Formulation Interview?
choices: A set of DSM-5 questions about how a person understands their problem
check.why: It gives clinicians questions about a person's own view of their problem and what help they want.

check.q: What does culturally responsive care do?
choices: Respects a person's beliefs while offering evidence-based treatment
check.why: It honors culture and beliefs while offering treatments with evidence.

lessons.title: 988 and School Supports
lessons.mainIdea: Help is close: 988 is available any time, and schools have trained people ready to listen.
reading: On a night when a friend texts that they feel hopeless, it helps to know what to do. In July 2022 the United States launched *988*, a three-digit number for the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. Anyone can call or text 988, or chat online, any time of day. Trained counselors listen and help people find safety and support. You can also call for a friend.

Schools have supports too. A *school counselor* helps with stress, friendships and plans. School psychologists and social workers can help with learning, emotions and family needs. Many schools use a *safety plan*, a short written list of warning signs, calming steps, people to contact and places to go. In an emergency, call 911.

Helping a friend can be simple. Listen without judging. Take what they say seriously. Stay with them, and tell a trusted adult, even if they asked you to keep it secret. You are not expected to fix everything. Your job is to connect your friend to someone who can help. Reaching out for yourself is also a strong and healthy choice.

words.d: the three-digit number to call or text the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, any time
a trained staff member who helps students with stress, relationships and plans
a short written list of warning signs, calming steps, people to contact and places to go

look.title: Map Your Support
look.text: Draw three circles. Inner circle: people you can talk to any day. Middle circle: adults at school who can help, like a counselor or nurse. Outer circle: help available any time, such as 988 by call or text, and 911 in an emergency.
look.prompt: Who is in each of your circles? If one circle is empty, what is one step you could take to fill it?

check.q: When did the 988 Lifeline number launch?
check.why: The three-digit 988 number launched in July 2022.

check.q: How can a person reach 988?
choices: Call, text or chat, any time
check.why: Anyone can call, text or chat with 988 any time of day.

check.q: A friend says they feel hopeless and asks you to keep it secret. What does the reading say to do?
choices: Keep the secret no matter what
Listen, stay with them and tell a trusted adult
check.why: The reading says to listen, take it seriously, stay with them and tell a trusted adult.

review.q: What did Dorothea Dix use to persuade lawmakers in 1843?
choices: Careful, detailed evidence from her visits
review.why: Dix recorded towns and conditions visit by visit and presented a memorial.

review.q: Put in order: Dix's memorial, the Community Mental Health Act, the 988 launch.
review.why: Dix wrote in 1843, Kennedy signed the Act in 1963, and 988 launched in 2022.

review.q: Which treatment teaches people to spot and change unhelpful thoughts?
review.why: CBT, developed by Aaron Beck, works on thoughts, feelings and actions.

review.q: Which statement about addiction matches the chapter?
choices: It is a treatable brain condition, and recovery is possible
review.why: NIDA describes addiction as a treatable brain disorder; many people recover.

review.q: How does the neurodiversity view approach different minds?
choices: With respect for natural variety and with accommodations
By trying to make everyone the same
review.why: Neurodiversity stresses respect and supports such as accommodations.

review.q: How is modern mindfulness different from its Buddhist roots?
choices: Programs like MBSR teach it in a nonreligious way
review.why: In Buddhism it is part of a spiritual path; MBSR teaches it without religion.

review.q: Why might a doctor use the Cultural Formulation Interview?
choices: To learn how a patient understands their own problem
review.why: It asks how a person understands their problem and what help they want.

review.q: Which is a helpful way to support a friend who is struggling?
choices: Tell them to snap out of it
Listen, take them seriously and connect them with a trusted adult or 988
review.why: The chapter says to listen, stay with them and connect them to help.
